support.quote: We went into the fight with 386, all told — 358 guns. Every pioneer and musician who could carry a musket went into the ranks
support.note: Chamberlain, report of 6 July 1863 (four days after): "We went into the fight with 386, all told — 358 guns. Every pioneer and musician who could carry a musket went into the ranks." He adds that the sick and foot-sore who had fallen behind came up and took their places in line, and that men under sentence of court-martial were put into the fight. So 386 counts every man who went into the line of battle; 358 counts those with muskets. He does not say who the other 28 were.

weighing.summary: The only count by a man who counted his own regiment is Chamberlain's: 386 all told, 358 guns, written four days after, saying what is in each. Barnes's 380, written 53 days after from the brigade's reports and from outside the regiment, is a relay. Fox's table gives 386 with no source and is counted with Chamberlain. The regiment's survivors take 358 as the number engaged on the monument and in Melcher; Gerrish and the Maine volume say about 350. The plan's 385 has no source anywhere. So 386 men, 358 of them with muskets, is the best-supported figure, weighted not settled because only Chamberlain gives it and nobody confirms it independently.
weighing.who: Chamberlain commanded the regiment and counted its men; Barnes commanded the division and was elsewhere; Fox compiled a table from returns without naming a source for this entry; Melcher and Gerrish were in the regiment (an officer and a private); the monument committee and the Maine commission wrote later for the veterans.
weighing.when: Chamberlain wrote four days after (best class and nearest to the count); Barnes 53 days; the monument 23 years; Melcher 25; Gerrish 19; the Maine volume 35; Fox 26 years after. A report of the time outranks later memory, and the later writers who give 358 or 350 are using the muskets figure or a round number.
weighing.where: Chamberlain was in the line and knew who came up (the sick and foot-sore, the pioneers and musicians, the men under sentence); the others counted from outside or from memory.
weighing.how_knew: Chamberlain gives his own breakdown (all told against guns) and says who is in it; Barnes names his source in general (the brigade's reports) without a number; Fox names none; Melcher and Gerrish remember; the monument and Maine volume repeat the musket figure or a round one.
weighing.clock: Not applicable to a count. The count is of the men who went into the fight in the late afternoon of 2 July; the reported 20-minute difference between the armies' clocks bears on no figure.
weighing.independence: One line of knowledge carries 386: Chamberlain's report (Fox's 386 is counted with it, and Norton prints the same report), so the default is flagged single-source. 358 is Chamberlain's own musket count; the monument and Melcher give 358 as the regiment's number or men engaged, the same figure, and a copy from him is likely but not stated. Barnes is one witness who relays the brigade's reports. Gerrish and the Maine volume are round figures from two writers.

what_would_change_it: The 20th Maine's muster-out rolls or the Maine adjutant general's roll of the men present on 2 July, or Prince's list of the companies present, would give a count that does not depend on Chamberlain's word. A report of the brigade's strength on 30 June 1863 at regimental level would check both 386 and 380. A source for the plan's 385 would add that value.
